title: Mashreq Launches NEO BIZ Digital Banking Platform for Pakistan SMEs
snippet: The Dubai-headquartered bank is targeting Pakistan's 7.14 million MSMEs with an integrated digital business banking platform including payments, payroll and BaaS. The post Mashreq Launches NEO BIZ Digital Banking Platform for Pakistan SMEs appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Mashreq has launched NEO BIZ in Pakistan, a digital business banking proposition aimed at the country’s small and medium-sized enterprise segment. The platform is designed to provide integrated account management, payments, collections and a roadmap of additional services to sole proprietors, self-employed individuals and registered SMEs, without requiring branch visits for routine transactions.

Pakistan’s MSME sector is substantial but structurally underbanked. The country’s roughly 7.14 million micro, small and medium-sized enterprises account for nearly 40 per cent of GDP, 30 per cent of exports and more than 80 per cent of non-agricultural employment. Yet outstanding SME financing stood at approximately PKR 882 billion as of December 2025, a figure that reflects both recent credit expansion and the scale of the gap that remains. Mashreq is positioning NEO BIZ to serve that unmet demand through digital channels rather than a branch-heavy model.

What the platform offers

At launch, NEO BIZ provides digital account opening, payments and collections within a single interface. The near-term roadmap adds business debit and virtual cards, payroll, invoice-based payments, transaction analytics and bookkeeping. Longer-term, Mashreq intends to layer Banking-as-a-Service infrastructure on top of the core product, enabling third-party integrations covering supply chain finance, tax facilitation and cash flow-based lending. The phased build-out is consistent with a BaaS model that seeks to become an operational platform rather than a standalone current account.

Muhammad Hamayun Sajjad, chief executive of Mashreq Bank Pakistan, framed the launch as addressing three specific gaps: access, awareness and digital capability. “With NEO BIZ, we are introducing a platform that is built specifically for the realities of this market, one that simplifies banking, reduces dependency on physical channels and supports businesses as they grow,” he said.

Distribution will combine digital onboarding with what the bank describes as phygital touchpoints, meaning a hybrid of physical agent or partner points and digital workflows, alongside strategic commercial partnerships. No specific distribution partners were named in the announcement.

Market context and competitive read-across

Pakistan’s digital banking landscape has been moving quickly. The State Bank of Pakistan issued its first five digital retail bank licences in 2023 and 2024, and several of those newly licensed entities are targeting the SME and micro-business segment alongside consumer retail. Mashreq enters as an established international bank with an existing local licence rather than as a new challenger, which gives it a regulatory head start but means it is competing not only with incumbent commercial banks but with better-capitalised, digitally native entrants.

The BaaS ambition is the most strategically significant element of the announcement. Across South and Southeast Asia, several regional banks have attempted to replicate the platform-banking model pioneered by fintechs, integrating payroll, invoicing and supply chain tools to increase switching costs and deepen wallet share among small businesses. Execution risk is material: the businesses Mashreq is targeting often operate informally, making credit assessment and digital onboarding more complex than the product framing implies.

Fernando Morillo, Mashreq’s group head of retail banking, cited the bank’s cross-market experience as a differentiator, arguing that digital-first banking models had demonstrably improved efficiency and transparency for businesses in other markets where Mashreq operates. Pakistan will test whether a model refined in the Gulf can translate to a market with a different regulatory environment, infrastructure maturity and SME formality profile. The bank has not disclosed a target customer number or a revenue projection for the Pakistan business.

title: Mastercard Extends First-Party Trust Fraud Programme to Europe
snippet: Mastercard is rolling out its chargeback-dispute programme to Europe from July 2027, targeting a projected 324 million global chargeback transactions by 2028. The post Mastercard Extends First-Party Trust Fraud Programme to Europe appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Mastercard has announced the European expansion of its First-Party Trust programme, which is designed to help merchants and card issuers distinguish genuine third-party fraud from first-party misuse, the practice commonly called “friendly fraud” where a cardholder disputes a legitimate purchase either deliberately or because they fail to recognise a transaction on their statement.

The rollout covers Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa from October 2026, with full European availability scheduled for July 2027. The programme had already been live in the United States, Canada, Latin America, the Caribbean and Asia Pacific since 2024.

How the programme works

Michele Centemero,EVP of services Europe at Mastercard

First-Party Trust operates through two parallel mechanisms. The first feeds Mastercard’s fraud-risk models into the authorisation flow, generating signals that flag transactions most consistent with third-party fraud and tag those carrying higher levels of transactional trust. The second allows merchants to submit supporting evidence during the dispute process, including details of delivery, authentication and purchase history, enabling issuers to make a more granular determination about whether a chargeback claim is legitimate.

Merchants who meet the programme’s evidence-sharing requirements receive chargeback protection on qualifying disputes, creating a direct commercial incentive to participate. Small businesses are explicitly included in the scope, which is a meaningful detail given that chargeback costs are proportionally heavier for lower-volume merchants.

Michele Centemero, executive vice president of services Europe at Mastercard, said: “By helping merchants and issuers access relevant transaction information needed to review disputed purchases, we can reduce unnecessary disputes while strengthening confidence across the payments ecosystem.”

Market context

The commercial pressure underlying the programme is substantial. Global chargeback volume is forecast to reach 324 million transactions in 2028, up from a 2025 estimate of 261 million, according to the Merchant Risk Council. That trajectory reflects both the continued growth of card-not-present commerce and a documented rise in deliberate first-party misuse, which industry estimates have long suggested accounts for a meaningful share of total dispute volume but is difficult to separate from genuine fraud in conventional dispute workflows.

The European payments landscape adds a regulatory dimension. The EU’s revised Payment Services Directive (PSD2) and its successor PSD3 place specific obligations on issuers and payment service providers around fraud liability and dispute resolution. Any tooling that improves the evidential basis for issuer decisions carries compliance value beyond the commercial case alone. Merchants operating under Strong Customer Authentication rules already generate authentication data that the First-Party Trust framework can repurpose as compelling evidence, which reduces the incremental burden of participation.

Visa has long maintained its own dispute-resolution and chargeback management infrastructure, including Visa Resolve Online and the Compelling Evidence 3.0 framework it introduced in 2023. Mastercard’s expansion brings First-Party Trust broadly into alignment with what the competing network offers merchants and issuers in terms of structured evidence submission. The competitive dynamic means that issuers managing both Mastercard and Visa portfolios will now have analogous, though not identical, tools across their card books, which simplifies internal workflows even if it does not eliminate complexity.

The practical test for the European rollout will be adoption rates among acquirers and their merchant bases. Network programmes of this kind require acquirer buy-in to surface cleanly in merchant integrations, and the July 2027 general availability date gives acquirers roughly nine months from now to build or update their dispute-handling flows.

A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing.

  

            						

The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.

The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.

The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'

The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.

Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.

Notes to editors

Read more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.

The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.

The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.

As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.

The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

title: Global Payments faces industry pricing pressure
snippet: While analysts point to an increasingly competitive environment for the processor, the company is still trying to raise prices.
fullText:
Global Payments and other processors face an increasingly competitive market, with rising pricing pressures forcing some businesses in the ecosystem to consider consolidation.

Global Payments has touted increased merchant acceptance of its Genius point-of-sale services brand, but now it may be trying to force through price hikes in an increasingly competitive market.

The payments processing company is seeking to implement a new $699 annual fee for its merchant clients next month, according to a merchant consultant who posted a portion of a Global Payments letter on LinkedIn. 

“Worldpay, now part of Global Payments, is introducing a $699 annual fee, with the first charge hitting merchant statements this December. Yes, another one,” Merchant Cost Consulting Partner Matt Rej said in the LinkedIn post last week. “And this is on top of the other increases we've already seen from Worldpay this year.”

Rej questioned, and poked fun at, the reasoning Global Payments provided for the increase, pointing to the company’s letter saying: “Government and industry regulations have had a significant impact on system requirements in the payment processing industry.”

The Atlanta-based company didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Nonetheless, in its third-quarter earnings press release last week, the company acknowledged “increased competition in the markets in which we operate.”

Global Payments pricing moves come less than a year after it completed its $24.25 billion purchase of the merchant services company Worldpay, which could give the company stronger pricing power in the industry. In the third-quarter report, Global Payments reported that the Genius brand, which was launched last year, was placed at 65% more merchant locations, compared to the year-earlier period, and bookings more than doubled.   

As the Genius brand gains traction, the company is reportedly considering selling itself off to one of its largest shareholders, private equity firm GTCR, and the investment firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice. GTCR is acquainted with Global Payments partly because it was one of the companies that sold it the Worldpay assets.

Any fee increases by POS service providers are increasingly met with pressure from younger financial technology companies building a presence in the market with newer technologies. As a result, some legacy companies that provide payments services to merchants, including behemoth Fiserv, the new entrant Shift4 and the Dutch company Adyen, are feeling a competitive crunch.

Point-of-sale services firm PayCompass said in September that it had merged with two other firms and the CEO at the merchant services provider Butter Payments said last month that the company had sold its assets to an unnamed buyer.

While analysts who follow Global Payments praised the company’s progress in integrating Worldpay into its operations and luring merchants to the Genius brand, they noted the increasingly competitive market. As such, price increases may be a tough sell, particularly as merchants face consumers stretched by inflationary pressures. 

Analysts at the investment firm William Blair raised concerns about Global Payments technology being capable of competing with new fintechs.

“While sales metrics appear strong, we argue Genius is simply not a competitive offering from a technology standpoint and will not become material enough to durably accelerate consolidated organic growth,” the analysts said in a Thursday note to their clients, acknowledging the brand’s third-quarter growth.

Other analysts who follow the company also pointed out the competitive intensity in the market in commenting on Global Payments results.

“The Payments industry is very competitive with both existing and emerging competition,” analysts for TD Cowen told clients in a note Thursday. “All of our companies face the risk of being unable to capture market share or having their business models become commoditized by newer entrants in the market. Additionally, our companies are levered to consumer spending and therefore are exposed to general economic conditions.”

Analysts who follow the company for the investment firm R.W. Baird called out the difficulties for raising prices at this time across the industry. “Pricing pressure is a constant threat, and new fintechs have become competitive threats as well,” analysts at the Baird Equity Research arm said in a Thursday note. 

A sale to private owners might relieve some of the pressure of operating in the publicly traded market, with its focus on quarterly reports. Still, the analysts at William Blair last week gave the deal less than a 50-50 chance of being completed, partly because of the debt that Global Payments has in the wake of its Worldpay deal.

In a prior Oct. 30 note focused exclusively on the reports of a potential Global Payments sale, the William Blair analysts said that some $22 billion of debt at the company “could be an impediment, especially in a rising rate environment.”

The William Blair analysts posited that they could be wrong about the chances of the sale. If they are, they forecast that other “debt-laden” publicly traded companies in the industry, including Shift4 Payments and Fiserv, will see “pressure to sell will ratchet up dramatically, setting up what could be the final wave of industry consolidation.”

title: FSE Group Launches £70m Future London Growth Fund for SMEs
snippet: The FSE Group has launched a new debt fund backed by the British Business Bank and Funding London to close London's SME scale-up The post FSE Group Launches £70m Future London Growth Fund for SMEs appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The FSE Group has launched the Future London Growth Fund, a debt vehicle targeting over £70 million in lending to London-based scale-up businesses that struggle to access growth capital from mainstream lenders. Cornerstone commitments have been provided by the British Business Bank, which committed £20 million, and Funding London, the Mayor of London’s investment arm, which invested through its GLIF Limited entity.

The fund offers individual loans of between £1 million and £3 million, a ticket size positioned in the gap between standard bank finance and larger venture debt facilities. It is open to companies with strong commercial traction and credible growth plans but which may not yet be profitable. Applications are now open across all 32 London boroughs and the City of London.

The lending gap it targets

The structural problem the fund is designed to address is well documented. Research from the British Business Bank’s “Alone Together” report found that London is the toughest place in the UK to be an entrepreneur: only 71% of London-based business owners reported a profit compared with a UK average of 84%. Entrepreneurs in economically deprived urban areas face compounding barriers to finance even when they are physically proximate to one of the world’s most developed investment ecosystems.

Puneet Raj Bhatia, managing director at Funding London, described the target cohort as businesses seeking deals too large for early-stage finance but routinely overlooked by mainstream lenders. That is a segment the British Business Bank has been trying to address through its regional investment funds for several years, with FSE already managing the £66 million debt portion of Funding London’s Greater London Investment Fund since 2019. The new fund is a direct continuation of that regional strategy.

Kala Desai, head of the Future London Growth Fund at FSE, said: “London is home to an exceptional community of high-growth, innovative businesses, yet many still hit a barrier when accessing scale-up capital.”

FSE’s track record and market context

FSE brings a substantial operational base to the fund. The firm manages approaching £460 million across its fund portfolio, has backed over 1,000 scaling businesses and reports that £300 million of its invested capital has helped portfolio companies leverage an additional £780 million in private funding. It also manages debt tranches within the British Business Bank’s South West Investment Fund, Investment Fund for Scotland, Midlands Engine Investment Fund and the newly awarded South East Investment Fund.

The broader market for public-private SME debt in the UK has expanded steadily since the British Business Bank’s inception in 2014. In its 2025-26 financial year the Bank supported £9.4 billion in finance to smaller businesses, crowding in £4.3 billion of private capital alongside £1.3 billion of public funding. The Future London Growth Fund sits within that architecture, applying a regionally focused, relationship-led model that has become increasingly common as public development banks seek to direct capital into underserved geographies rather than relying on commercial lenders to self-allocate.

The competitive context is relevant for advisers directing borrowers toward this type of facility. Growth lending in the £1 million to £3 million range is also covered by a range of challenger banks and specialist lenders, several of which have increased their UK regional presence in recent years. What the FSE model emphasises is the relationship and network element, rather than a purely automated credit decisioning approach, which may be an advantage for businesses that have non-standard financial profiles.

The next markers to watch are deployment pace, the sector mix of the initial cohort of borrowers, and whether the fund attracts further private capital commitments beyond its public cornerstone investors.

title: Glovo and PragmaGO Bring Embedded Lending to Polish Merchants
snippet: PragmaCash is now available to Glovo's restaurant and retail partners in Poland, offering financing of up to PLN 100,000 within one business day. The post Glovo and PragmaGO Bring Embedded Lending to Polish Merchants appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Glovo and PragmaGO have extended their embedded lending partnership to Poland, making PragmaCash financing available to the delivery platform’s network of local merchants from October 2026. Poland is the third market for the tie-up, following rollouts in Spain and Romania.

The product targets the small and independent businesses that make up a significant share of Glovo’s merchant base: restaurants, cafés, grocery stores, florists and pharmacies. Merchants can apply entirely online, receive a credit decision within minutes, and access financing of up to PLN 100,000 (approximately EUR 23,000), with funds transferred to their account within one business day. The financing carries no stated restriction on use, meaning it can cover stock purchases, seasonal staffing or any other operational need.

The commercial case

Joanna Budzik-Lister, VP strategic partnerships at PragmaGO

Joanna Budzik-Lister, VP strategic partnerships at PragmaGO, pointed to internal data as the backbone of the commercial argument. “Our data show that companies using this type of financing achieve year-on-year turnover that is 28% higher than companies that do not use it,” she said. The comparison is drawn from PragmaGO’s Merchant Cash Advance cohort, tracking the twelve months before and after a financing application.

Diana Hangartner, commercial director at Glovo Poland

Diana Hangartner, commercial director at Glovo Poland, framed the partnership as extending the platform’s existing value proposition beyond logistics. Running a local business now requires the capacity to act quickly on market opportunities, she said, and access to capital through the platform itself reduces friction for merchants already operating inside the Glovo ecosystem.

PragmaGO reported that nearly 24,000 entrepreneurs used its embedded lending product in 2025, drawing a combined PLN 872 million (approximately EUR 200 million) in financing across its markets. That figure represents a 66% year-on-year increase, though the release did not break down volume by country.

Market context

Embedded lending for gig-economy and delivery platform merchants has become a competitive category across Europe. The model is structurally attractive: a platform that processes a merchant’s transaction data already holds the most reliable proxy for repayment capacity, making underwriting faster and cheaper than a traditional bank loan application. Several other platform lenders and banking-as-a-service providers are pursuing the same merchant segments, including through partnerships with food-delivery and e-commerce marketplaces.

PragmaGO’s positioning is notable in that it is not a pure-play technology intermediary but a regulated financial institution with three decades of SME lending experience in Poland, operating since 1996. The group’s structure, which includes a Romanian digital factoring subsidiary, a Spanish embedded-finance unit and a Croatian operation, suggests a deliberate multi-market expansion model rather than an opportunistic single-deal play. That breadth of regulated experience may give it a compliance advantage as EU supervisors pay closer attention to the non-bank lending layer sitting inside consumer-facing platforms.

Poland’s SME financing market is large and historically underserved by retail banks for short-term working capital, which creates structural demand for faster, data-driven alternatives. The Glovo distribution channel gives PragmaGO a captive merchant population with verifiable revenue data, while Glovo gains a value-added service that deepens merchant retention without requiring it to hold a lending licence itself. The next test is whether transaction volumes in Poland match the trajectory seen in Spain and Romania, and whether the product can be scaled without a material rise in default rates as the borrower pool widens.

title: Onramper Launches Chrome Extension for Crypto Quote Comparison
snippet: The Amsterdam fiat-to-crypto aggregator is bringing live quotes from 30+ licensed providers into Chrome's side panel for in-browser buying. The post Onramper Launches Chrome Extension for Crypto Quote Comparison appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Onramper, the Amsterdam-based fiat-to-crypto onramp aggregator, has launched a Chrome browser extension that lets users compare live crypto purchase quotes from more than thirty licensed providers without navigating away from their current page. The extension is available now on the Chrome Web Store.

The product surfaces in Chrome’s side panel, pulling quotes from Onramper’s existing provider network and displaying them alongside one another in the user’s local currency. Users can buy, sell or swap, select their preferred provider and complete a transaction without opening a new tab. Onramper and the chosen provider handle identity verification and payment processing at checkout. The extension supports more than 170 local payment methods, including card, bank transfer, Apple Pay and Google Pay, with availability varying by country.

How it works

Rick Thomas, co-CEO at Onramper

The extension is positioned as a comparison layer, not a standalone exchange. Users who connect a wallet can also swap tokens directly from the panel. Up to five wallet addresses can be saved under custom names, with a one-click copy function at checkout. Localised currency display and preset transaction amounts are applied automatically based on the user’s country.

Privacy features include no embedded analytics or tracking. Settings and saved wallet addresses are stored locally in the browser, with cross-device sync disabled by default and a single-action data-erasure option in the settings menu.

Onramper co-chief executive Rick Thomas framed the launch as a structural shift in how crypto access is delivered. “Crypto has treated the on-ramp as a destination: a separate site, a separate tab, a separate decision. As the industry matures, buying has to happen where people already are, and with more providers and payment methods in every market, comparing them should not be a research project,” he said.

Onramper’s existing client list includes Exodus, Coinbase, Jupiter, Kraken and pump.fun, providing the company with meaningful distribution through its widget and API business before this consumer-facing extension.

Market context

The fiat-to-crypto onramp segment has consolidated around a small number of aggregators over the past two years, with players such as MoonPay, Transak and Ramp Network competing alongside Onramper for integrations with wallets and Web3 applications. The browser-extension route is a distinct channel rather than a direct challenge to those B2B integrations: it targets end users directly and reduces friction at the point of discovery rather than at the point of application onboarding.

That consumer-facing angle carries regulatory considerations that the B2B widget business largely bypasses. Direct-to-user crypto purchasing tools must comply with the applicable financial promotion rules in each jurisdiction. In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority‘s crypto financial promotions regime, which came into full effect in 2024, imposes strict approval requirements on the marketing of qualifying cryptoassets. The EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation introduces further conduct obligations for firms serving retail customers across member states. The extension’s routing model, in which Onramper aggregates and displays quotes but the selected licensed provider executes the transaction, may limit Onramper’s direct regulatory exposure in some markets, though that determination will depend on how individual regulators characterise the aggregation activity.

The near-term measure of success for the extension will be

adoption volume and whether the browser channel converts browsers into buyers at a meaningfully higher rate than tab-switching behaviour currently allows. Onramper has not disclosed a target user number or a timeline for expanding availability beyond Chrome.

title: Tipalti Launches AP Agent with MCP Links to Enterprise AI Tools
snippet: Tipalti's next-generation AP Agent coordinates the full accounts payable lifecycle, while new MCP capabilities connect live financial data to tools including Claude The post Tipalti Launches AP Agent with MCP Links to Enterprise AI Tools appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Tipalti has announced AP Agent, a next-generation agentic AI product designed to manage the complete accounts payable lifecycle, from invoice capture and coding through to approvals, payments and reconciliation. The Foster City-based company, which processes more than $100 billion in annualised payment volume across 120 currencies for around 6,500 customers, has also introduced Model Context Protocol (MCP) capabilities that connect its financial data to enterprise AI tools such as Claude Enterprise.

The announcement extends work Tipalti began in 2025 when it introduced a first generation of specialised AI agents. AP Agent represents a step change in scope: rather than automating discrete tasks, it is designed to orchestrate entire workflows, drawing on vendor history, general ledger data and company-specific accounting policies to make context-aware decisions rather than following static rule sets.

Human oversight at the centre

Roby Baruch, chief product and technology officer at Tipalti

The product is built around what Tipalti describes as a configurable human-in-the-loop model. Finance teams can define which activities the agent executes autonomously and which require a human sign-off, with field-level reasoning surfaced to explain AI-generated values. Every action is logged in a full audit trail, and users can interrogate, clarify or override individual decisions through natural-language conversation. The company says the agent applies corrections from user feedback to future processing, improving accuracy over time.

Roby Baruch, chief product and technology officer at Tipalti, said the company’s aim is to give finance leaders “the confidence to reimagine what their teams and their businesses can achieve” as AI agents take on more autonomous responsibilities. Tipalti did not publish independent benchmark data for processing accuracy or straight-through reconciliation rates in the announcement.

MCP and the data connectivity play

The MCP addition is arguably the more structurally significant element. By implementing the Model Context Protocol, Tipalti allows its AP and payments data to be queried in real time through external AI tools without manual exports or platform switching. Paired with an ERP connection such as NetSuite, the capability can support month-end reconciliation, custom reporting dashboards and payment-term SLA tracking.

Tipalti says its existing security framework, including OFAC screening, SOC-compliant data protection and role-based access controls, carries over to the MCP layer, a point that will matter to compliance and treasury teams weighing whether to authorise the connection.

Market context and regulatory read-across

The agentic AI push in finance operations is intensifying. Several established AP automation vendors, alongside newer AI-native entrants, are competing on the same axis of autonomous workflow execution with human oversight. The meaningful differentiators at this stage are the depth of financial controls embedded in the agent, the breadth of payment rails and currency coverage, and the quality of ERP integrations. Tipalti’s scale and its banking partnerships with Citi, Wells Fargo, J.P. Morgan and Visa give it distribution leverage that earlier-stage rivals cannot easily replicate.

On the regulatory side, agentic AI in finance is entering a period of active scrutiny. The EU’s AI Act classifies certain uses of AI in financial decision-making as high-risk, with obligations around transparency, logging and human oversight. Tipalti’s emphasis on explainability and audit trails is aligned with those requirements, though firms deploying the agent in regulated contexts will need to satisfy their own compliance teams that the model’s decision logic meets internal governance standards. In the UK, the FCA‘s broader AI strategy and its ongoing work on algorithmic systems in financial services will also shape how enterprise buyers assess the risk appetite involved in expanding autonomous AP execution.

title: Circle Exec Frames USDC as Consumer Utility, Not Financial Tool
snippet: Circle's chief product officer Nikhil Chandhok argues the winning stablecoin will be the one easiest for billions to use. The post Circle Exec Frames USDC as Consumer Utility, Not Financial Tool appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Circle‘s chief product and technology officer Nikhil Chandhok is making a deliberately unfashionable argument about stablecoins: that the technical architecture matters far less than whether an ordinary person with a phone can use USDC without knowing what a blockchain is.

Nikhil Chandhok, CPTO at Circle

Speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco and in a subsequent interview with Fintech Nexus, Chandhok drew on two decades of consumer-product experience at Google, YouTube and Meta to argue that stablecoin adoption will be determined by design, not by protocol competition.

“Everyone thinks about stablecoins as a financial instrument,” he said. “I think about it as a consumer problem.”

The consumer-product frame

Chandhok’s career makes the framing credible. He launched the YouTube app on the first iPhone in 2007, helped build YouTube Music into the platform’s top revenue driver and led Meta‘s augmented reality glasses programme before joining Circle. His read is that consumer technology succeeds when it delivers a concrete improvement in someone’s life without asking them to understand how it works.

Applied to USDC, the target use case is not sophisticated DeFi users but the Brazilian entrepreneur paying a Chinese supplier, the migrant worker sending a remittance, or the small business in a dollar-scarce market trying to hedge local currency risk. For those users, access to dollars via a smartphone is, as Chandhok put it, a ten- or hundred-times improvement over the status quo. The complexity of on-chain settlement is irrelevant if it is invisible.

He identified two design principles he said are frequently misapplied. The first is simplicity: do not explain how the product works; demonstrate the value it delivers. The second is network utility: treat a stablecoin network the way engineers treat a communications protocol, where every new participant makes the system more useful for all existing participants, rather than as a financial tool to be optimised in isolation.

“If you reason about the problem as a network utility instead of treating it as a financial tool, you build products differently,” Chandhok said, noting that getting this framing backwards has derailed many design teams.

Regulatory and competitive context

The argument arrives at a significant moment for stablecoin regulation. In the US, the GENIUS Act and related Senate proposals have moved stablecoin legislation closer to the floor than at any point since Facebook’s Libra project prompted a Congressional backlash in 2019. In the EU, MiCA is now in force, and e-money token issuers face reserve, redemption and marketing requirements that directly shape the consumer-product decisions Chandhok is describing. Circle received an EU e-money institution licence in 2024, positioning USDC ahead of competitors in compliant European distribution.

USDC is the second-largest stablecoin by market capitalisation, behind Tether‘s USDT. Tether has historically dominated emerging-market remittance and informal dollar corridors precisely because of its early distribution. Chandhok’s consumer-product thesis is partly a claim that Circle can compete on user experience where it cannot yet compete on network scale, and that regulatory clarity in Western markets will eventually redraw the competitive map.

The near-term test is whether programmability, which Chandhok flagged as a further differentiator, translates into adoption in agentic AI workflows, where autonomous software agents need to settle transactions without human sign-off. Circle has positioned USDC as infrastructure for that use case, though the market for AI-to-AI payments remains nascent and largely unregulated.

title: Western Union, Intermex clash
snippet: The money transfer services company dropped its acquisition of the smaller rival after California regulators weighed in, but now a fight over the deal has ensued.
fullText:
Remittance services provider Western Union planned to buy International Money Express, but opted out Tuesday. Now, the two companies have begun a battle over whether the $500 million deal should be consummated.

Western Union had been waiting more than a year for regulators to approve a purchase of the younger rival also known as Intermex, but when the California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation issued approval conditions Tuesday, the acquirer backed out. Western Union decided against the deal and notified Intermex it was terminating the acquisition agreement on Tuesday, the day that was the deadline for either side to exit the pact.

The California regulator “delivered unacceptable final Conditions of Approval that would have required material changes to Western Union’s business model, its agent relationships and execution of its long-term business strategy,” Western Union said in a press release late Tuesday. 

Western Union’s move isn’t passing muster with Intermex, which notified Western Union on Wednesday that it expects the transaction to be completed. Now, a legal fight is brewing.

“Through its counsel, Intermex has responded to Western Union rejecting Western Union's purported termination of the merger agreement and demanding that Western Union take all actions necessary to consummate the merger,” Intermex said in its statement.

Denver-based Western Union, which provides cross-border payments services and has roots reaching back more than 100 years, announced in August 2025 that it would purchase Intermex, but since then the companies have been trying to gather needed regulatory approvals. Miami-based Intermex was founded in 1994.

“Western Union stands by its decision to terminate the merger agreement and disagrees with Intermex’s characterization of the termination,” a spokesperson for Western Union said by email. “Western Union believes it acted in accordance with the terms of the agreement and will respond as appropriate.”

While New York regulators reached an agreement with the companies for approval of the deal earlier this year, the companies still needed California’s input, given the states’ purview over money transfer businesses.

The California agency approved the deal Tuesday, but imposed conditions that it said were aimed at safeguarding consumers, preventing fraud, deterring money laundering and ensuring “ fair and competitive access to financial services.”

California called Western Union a major money transfer company used by Californians to send money to Mexico and Central America, but it also noted that Intermex is a significant player in the market, saying the merger would have “significant implications for California consumers.” 

To consummate the merger, the state regulator said in a Tuesday statement that the companies must “take certain steps,” that it didn’t specify in its public statement, “to detect and deter fraud.” 

The regulator also prohibited the companies from reducing the number of agent locations that provide services in California.Citing an existing court order requiring Western Union to thwart criminal use of its network, the regulator also called on the company to “adopt robust risk-based anti-fraud and anti-money laundering measures.”

The state department also underscored its conditions with a threat. “If Western Union consummates its transaction with Intermex and fails to comply with these conditions, DFPI can take enforcement actions that may lead to limitations on its business practices or suspension of its license,” California’s statement said. 

The state noted federal immigration policies under the Trump administration have affected the market. That negative impact from reduced immigration movement that leads migrant workers to send money to friends and family was clear last week during Western Union’s third-quarter earnings report. 

“The last 18 months have been a difficult period for the remittance industry, particularly for those of us with relatively large retail franchises in the Americas,” Western Union CEO Devin McGranahan said during a webcast with analysts. “We have seen both an overall decline in the retail market and an acceleration of the shift towards digital.”

As part of its cost-cutting and shift to more digital operations, McGranahan said that Western Union had eliminated 500 full-time employees and has started a voluntary retirement program that it expects to lead to 150 more employee departures. 

At the end of last year, the company had about 9,600 workers worldwide, according to its annual filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

fullText:
Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.

The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.

Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.

That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.

Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.

Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.

What firms need to do now

So, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:

By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.

By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.

By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.

Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to: 

Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.

Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..

Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.

Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.

How we are supporting firms

We are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.

This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.

We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.

We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.

G7 Cyber Expert Group, Statement on advancing a coordinated roadmap for the transition to post-quantum cryptography in the financial sector

title: Finom adds MCP Connection for Claude and ChatGPT Account Queries
snippet: The European SME finance platform has launched a read-only Model Context Protocol link letting businesses query accounts from inside AI assistants. The post Finom adds MCP Connection for Claude and ChatGPT Account Queries appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Finom, the Amsterdam-headquartered financial platform for European SMEs, has launched Finom MCP, a read-only connection built on the open Model Context Protocol (MCP) standard that allows customers to query their Finom business accounts from inside Claude or ChatGPT using plain-language prompts.

The feature is included across all Finom plans and is rolling out pan-EU from today, 22 October 2026. At launch, customers can interrogate transactions, wallets, invoices, cards and accounting data, and request a morning briefing of recent business activity, without leaving their AI assistant.

What it does and what it deliberately does not

Kristjan Kaar, CPO at Finom

The read-only scope is a considered design choice rather than a capability gap. Both Claude and ChatGPT explicitly prohibit write actions that would result in money movement, and Finom’s own position is that trust in an AI-connected financial product must be established through progressive disclosure. The connection will not move funds, issue cards or alter account settings at launch.

Kristjan Kaar, Finom’s chief product officer, acknowledged that the company is not the first mover in this space. “We are not the first to public MCP and we will not pretend to be,” he said. “We’re starting with a first set of read-only access, with write capabilities to follow, all built on an open standard rather than a walled garden.”

Access is controlled entirely by the customer. The connection is initiated from within the assistant itself, redirecting users to a Finom-hosted consent screen where they authenticate with their existing Finom credentials. Role-scoped access means a user can only surface data their Finom account already permits them to see, and the connection can be revoked at any time. No credentials are passed to the AI provider.

Finom’s CAIO and co-founder Ivo Dimitrov framed the engineering priority as boundary design rather than model sophistication. “The engineering that matters here is not the model, it is the boundaries around it: your own login, access scoped to the role you already have, nothing shared beyond what you ask, and the ability to switch it off.”

The company is transparent that AI-generated answers may contain errors; the Finom app remains the authoritative record for official statements and reporting. Data retrieved through MCP is processed under the customer’s own agreement with their AI provider.

Market context and regulatory read-across

Finom’s own media FAQ names Qonto and Pennylane as firms that reached public MCP integrations first, which is an unusual degree of candour for a product launch announcement. The MCP standard, backed by Anthropic and gaining traction across enterprise tooling, is emerging as the practical mechanism by which AI assistants will connect to the business-software stack, much as OAuth became the standard handshake for web services. Early adoption of the open protocol, rather than building a proprietary integration, positions Finom to extend the connection to additional product areas without renegotiating closed partnerships.

For regulators, the architecture matters. Finom holds an Electronic Money Institution licence issued by De Nederlandsche Bank and operates within the EU’s PSD2 framework, which already mandates open APIs for account data access. An MCP layer built on top of regulated API access sits closer to the spirit of open finance than a screen-scraping or credential-sharing model. The phased approach, read access first, then user-confirmed write actions with secure authentication, mirrors the strong customer authentication logic that PSD2 and the incoming PSD3 regime apply to payment initiation.

Finom raised a 115 million euro Series C in June 2025, bringing total funding to more than 300 million euros. The company serves more than 300,000 businesses across Europe. The next phase of Finom MCP, in which the assistant prepares actions for the customer to confirm rather than simply answering questions, has no published timeline.

title: Rechitta V2 Adds Chat Mode after 100,000 Minutes of Broker Use
snippet: The Dubai proptech firm has launched a text-based chat mode alongside a rebuilt presentation experience, targeting real estate brokers handling live client queries. The post Rechitta V2 Adds Chat Mode after 100,000 Minutes of Broker Use appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Rechitta, a Dubai-based AI platform serving real estate brokers, has launched its V2 product update after recording 100,000 minutes of usage across its existing broker base. The milestone is being used by the company to validate the platform’s core proposition: replacing brochures, callback queues and scattered project documentation with a single AI-driven interface fed by verified developer data.

The V2 release centres on two interaction modes. Presentation Mode guides brokers through a project at their own pace, allowing them to scroll through visual assets and live project details while posing questions. The newly added Chat Mode is designed for situations where a spoken or guided session is impractical, such as when a broker is already on a call with a client or attending a busy sales event. Typed queries return instant answers on unit pricing, payment plans and handover dates, drawn from the same verified developer data that underpins the presentation layer.

Co-founder Aryaman Maheshwari said the 100,000-minute figure was significant because it reflected genuine engagement rather than passive sign-ups. “Those interactions have taught us how people actually want to explore, understand and question real estate projects,” he said. “V2 is a direct evolution of the product based on that behaviour.”

Co-founder Atiksh Mittal added that the update was intended to make the platform more conversational without removing the broker from the centre of the sales process.

The release also introduces the Rechitta Orb, a visual identity element the company says will serve as the recognisable interface for the AI assistant across both modes.

Market context

Rechitta sits within a broader category of AI-assisted sales enablement tools that have expanded quickly across Gulf real estate over the past two years. Dubai’s off-plan property market, which accounts for a substantial share of residential transaction volumes, creates particular information-management pressure: brokers routinely handle multiple concurrent project portfolios, each with distinct payment plan structures, handover schedules and unit availability that changes in near real time.

Several regional proptech firms and global CRM providers have moved to embed AI-powered Q&A and document-retrieval functions into broker workflows, though the verified-data angle Rechitta emphasises, where content originates directly from the developer rather than from scraped listings, represents a defensible point of differentiation if the developer onboarding pipeline can scale.

The broader regulatory environment for AI-powered sales tools in the UAE remains relatively permissive, with the Dubai Land Department actively encouraging digital transformation across the real estate transaction chain. However, the use of AI to communicate pricing and availability to brokers who then pass that information to buyers carries an implicit accuracy obligation, particularly as off-plan disputes in the emirate have drawn periodic regulatory attention.

Regulatory and commercial path

Rechitta has not disclosed the number of developers currently integrated onto the platform, the size of its broker user base, or whether it operates on a subscription, per-project or revenue-share commercial model. Those details matter for assessing whether 100,000 usage minutes represents a concentrated proof-of-concept with a small number of power users or a more distributed adoption curve across the market.

The next meaningful milestones to watch are developer count, geographic expansion beyond Dubai, and whether the company pursues external funding to accelerate integrations. Rechitta V2 is live now; a product walkthrough is available on the company’s website.

title: Stripe awaits payoff on Tempo chain
snippet: The company sees its Tempo blockchain as a key digital infrastructure play for the growing use of stablecoin transactions.
fullText:
Stripe entered the blockchain market last year with Tempo, a stablecoin-focused digital ledger it incubated – one of several ways the payment technology giant is trying to advance the cryptocurrencies.

Stripe further developed the blockchain business with Paradigm, a San Francisco-based venture capital fund. Then, the companies introduced Tempo in September 2025 with their initial partners artificial intelligence company Anthropic; food delivery provider DoorDash; and card network Visa. Today, companies use Tempo for remittances, cross-border payouts, and agentic commerce.

The startup has raised $500 million, giving it a $5 billion valuation, Fortune reported in October 2025. Tempo is led by Matt Huang, Paradigm’s co-founder and managing partner. Huang is also a director at Stripe and Kalshi, the online prediction exchange.

Dan Romero, a former Coinbase executive, is Tempo’s chief business officer. In a Nov. 6 interview, he discussed the blockchain’s origin, customers and the growing role of agentic payments.

Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.  

PAYMENTS DIVE: Stablecoins seem to have found a home in cross-border payments since the Genius Act. Are they being used anywhere else notably?

Optional Caption

Permission granted by Tempo

DAN ROMERO: There is a lot of trading that still happens with stablecoins. That was kind of the original use case. You pair a stablecoin with a crypto asset, and it's kind of a way to trade it. I think what has emerged over the last couple of years are what I would call real-world flows, flows that touch things that are not just crypto, (they’re) very much cross-border use cases. Remittance companies are very much leaning into stablecoins, traditional ones like Western Union and MoneyGram. Anyone who is moving money cross-border is taking a hard look at stablecoins because of that better, faster, cheaper nature, and that’s already a pretty competitive business from a kind of margin standpoint and cost. So, anytime you can actually improve efficiencies there – very compelling. A second component of cross-border, which is starting to pick up, is international payroll. 

And third … is just anyone who is moving a lot of money – they move it into their marketplace and then out of their marketplace to other bank accounts. They’re saying, “Why not offer a kind of embedded stablecoin wallet with the payout?” You can actually link a debit card, so it's really easy now to issue a virtual card off of any type of financial account that’s using stablecoins, and then it just appears in your Apple Pay, like any other card.

Is anyone doing this?

DoorDash is early to this, but DoorDash is an interesting marketplace because they have both the delivery drivers ... and the restaurants. You can imagine a world where DoorDash, not only in a country like the U.S., but they have operations all over the world. Stablecoins can move 24/7. They can move on the weekends. So you could imagine a future world where, when you complete a delivery working for DoorDash, you could get instantly paid out with a stablecoin into a wallet, where you may have a linked debit card, which means you can immediately go spend that, or the ability to have it go into an earned (deposit) program. Think of it as this modular financial infrastructure that’s quite flexible, and now in a post-Genius (Act) world, it’s regulated, and that's a good thing for enterprises.

It almost sounds like you're talking about a future where DoorDash, Amazon and the like become banks.

I would tweak that slightly. When you pay out a stablecoin to an embedded wallet, that's a self-custodial experience, and I think a lot of the infrastructure to make that seamless and feel just like a normal app – compared to crypto experiences from 10 years ago – there's been a lot of technology and infrastructure progression. Any marketplace you're paying someone out in stablecoin, the wallet that's holding the stablecoin, the user is fully in control. 

How did Tempo get started?

When I was at Coinbase, (the) 2014 era, Stripe was early to experimenting with bitcoin payments. In the early days, we thought bitcoin was going to be the new way to spend money online. In retrospect, (it’s) kind of obvious it was too volatile, too slow, too confusing for consumers. But Stripe was early, and experimented. It didn't work. They just shut it down. Sometimes experiment stuff doesn't work. The last couple years, Stripe has seen some of these early use cases that were more real world with stablecoins, and I think they were early to making a bet on stablecoins. They acquired Bridge actually before the Genius Act (Bridge sale was in October 2024). I don't think most people appreciate that. So, they were kind of skating to where the puck was going. But after acquiring Bridge and then Privy, which powers the wallets, I think Stripe realized that none of the blockchains that were out there were particularly well suited for at-scale payments.

Was that true or was that Stripe’s blockchain premise at the time?

I’d definitely say it was true. You couldn't get a normal payment, because everyone was trading. Think of it as (putting) Visa and the New York Stock Exchange together on the same database – you couldn’t get a payment through for six hours. It's just untenable for any company that’s trying to build on this stuff. … There's a lot of profit opportunity there. So, the willingness to pay on any given trade transaction is much higher than a payments transaction. Payments are low margin. Anytime there's actually a lot of activity happening on blockchain, payments get crowded out. Just a core premise: If you're in the business of doing both trading and payments, you are actually in the business of trading. Tempo reverses that structural level for the chain. We give 90% of the block space … to payments, the simple A-to-B transactions, and then the trades get put in second priority. That's actually worse for our business in terms of we make less money per transaction.

What’s the Tempo customer mix today?

Any company that would already do payments with Stripe. DoorDash is a good example. A lot of them, post-Genius, are now interested in stablecoins for some of the reasons we mentioned. Those companies kind of are our bread and butter in the sense that we're focused on payments. 

We have another category, which I would call … stablecoin savvy or stablecoin native. These are companies that already were using stablecoins, potentially pre-Genius, because they were startups. They were a little bit more comfortable with it, and I think that they've been uniquely enabled in growing their businesses by that. The third one, which is a bit more nascent, is agentic payments and AI and how do you actually play in that space? Our point of view is we're really, really early to agentic payments, and even three months ago, I'd have told you there’s basically none happening. I think it's materially changed in the last two months with Instinct and (Meta’s) Muse, and now I think the frontier labs are all basically going to have their own version of a personal agent assistant.

For the agent payments you mentioned, what are they being made with?

I would anticipate others are going to have more agentic payments in the next six to 12 months. I don't think it’s going to be a sleepy space. title: Vanquis Index: One-Third of Lower-Income UK Households Skip Meals
snippet: Vanquis's autumn 2026 Financial Wellbeing Index shows the score for households earning under £40,000 has fallen four points since May, to 64 out The post Vanquis Index: One-Third of Lower-Income UK Households Skip Meals appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Vanquis has published the autumn 2026 edition of its Financial Wellbeing Index, tracking households with an annual income of under £40,000. The index score for this group has fallen to 64 out of 100, down four points from 68 in May, against a two-point fall across the general population from 69 to 67. Both figures remain within the “moderate financial wellbeing” band, but the lower-income cohort is now at its lower edge and the gap between the two groups is widening.

The index draws on anonymised transaction data from a cohort of 58,263 lower-income households via the Snoop/SpendMapper platform, combined with a Mintel/Kantar consumer survey of 2,000 adults carried out between 23 September and 6 October 2026.

The pressures behind the numbers

The headline statistic likely to attract the most attention is food: 36% of lower-income households said they had skipped meals or reduced how much they ate in the previous three months due to financial pressure. A further 27% delayed medical or dental treatment they could not afford. Nearly half, 49%, said their financial situation had affected their mental wellbeing, the highest proportion since the research began and up from 42% in October 2024.

Financial headroom is thin. After spending and payments, including savings and debt repayments, lower-income households retained 4.6% of income in the latest quarter, slightly up from 4.5% the previous quarter. However, the amount going into savings fell 12.8% quarter on quarter, and one in four lower-income households hold no savings whatsoever, compared with 7% of higher-income households. The proportion who were able to reduce their debt fell from 59% in May to 48%, suggesting that households are finding it harder to strengthen their balance sheet through either saving or debt reduction.

Cost pressures are structural. Household bills overall are more than 10% higher than two years ago, with mortgage and rent up 24.1% over two years and water bills up 46.1% over the same period. Grocery spending has risen 7.8% over two years, despite households actively trading down: 75% of lower-income respondents are cutting non-essential spending, 66% are buying more own-label groceries, and 63% have moved to cheaper supermarkets. Even so, 44% of the cohort said they could not absorb a £100 rise in regular monthly costs without cutting essentials, using savings or borrowing.

Regulatory and market context

John Natalizia, deputy CEO at Vanquis

The Vanquis report lands in the context of heightened policy attention to financial vulnerability. The Financial Conduct Authority‘s Consumer Duty, now in its second year, requires lenders and financial services providers to demonstrate good outcomes for customers in vulnerable circumstances. The data here is directly relevant: the duty obliges firms to consider whether their products and services are genuinely affordable and to provide appropriate support when customers show signs of financial difficulty.

For Vanquis specifically, which is Bradford-headquartered, LSE-listed and serves 1.79 million customers through credit products and its Snoop money management platform, the index serves a dual purpose. It positions the firm as a voice on financial inclusion and social mobility while also surfacing the demand environment for its core market. A cohort in which 14% describe themselves as “struggling or in trouble” and only 18% say their finances are healthy represents both a need for appropriate lending products and a credit-risk consideration that the broader sector watches.

Looking ahead, 47% of lower-income respondents expect the cost-of-living situation to worsen over the next three months. Among those with financial concerns, just 6% have spoken to a financial adviser or debt counsellor, pointing to a persistent gap between need and access to professional support.

Deputy chief executive John Natalizia said: “Behind the figures are people trying to meet today’s commitments while worrying about tomorrow. Our responsibility is to understand those pressures and provide practical support that reflects people’s circumstances.”

title: Why PayPal wants to have a bank
snippet: The digital payments company would tap a bank subsidiary for lending to its merchants, but also to diversify its sources of capital.
fullText:
PayPal Holdings still sees advantages from winning a bank charter as the digital payments giant’s new CEO pursues a transformation of the company.

That’s according to the company’s chief financial and operating officer, Jamie Miller, who talked about PayPal’s bank charter application at the KBW Fintech Ecosystem Conference this week.

When Miller was asked by the analyst hosting the event to comment on PayPal’s effort to form an industrial bank, she explained how it would play into PayPal’s plan to provide more financial services, such as lending to its millions of merchant clients.

She pointed to the “merchant lending that underpins our work,” saying the company’s processing support for small businesses, sole proprietors and micro-sellers are all able to partake of its lending services.

San Jose, California-based PayPal filed applications with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and the Utah Department of Financial Institutions last December to establish a Utah-chartered industrial loan company back when Alex Chriss was CEO. But Chriss has since exited, with Enrique Lores taking that top post this past March.

Lores has continued to pursue a strategy offering more financial services to PayPal’s 400 million consumer customers and its 20 million merchant clients. Financial services that the company is spooling up include increased buy now, pay later lending under the PayPal Pay Later brand as well new services via its peer-to-peer payments tool Venmo. 

As part of PayPal’s restructuring plan begun in April, Lores has cut some 2,000 employee jobs, shaved management layers and reorganized the business into three key divisions: checkout and PayPal; consumer financial services and Venmo; and processing, payment services and crypto. 

The company expects to take about $1.5 billion in costs out of the business in the next two to three years, Miller said.

Miller also suggested a bank operation would be advantageous as another route to capital. “The other side of it is to diversify our funding sources,” she said at the event. 

“We've been building out a variety of different funding sources,” Miller said. “We fund a lot through our own free cash flow and our cash on balance sheet, but we've also begun taking books off balance sheet in Europe and in the U.S. to really just diversify where the cash and funding sources come from.”

Last year, PayPal sold the investment firm KKR some of its buy now, pay later loan receivables originated in France, Germany, the United Kingdom and other European countries. 

To the extent that a PayPal bank could take in consumer or commercial deposits that could also be a new source of capital, the CFO said. “Certainly, deposits are another cost-efficient way” to diversify the company’s capital sources, she said.

PayPal’s application for a bank charter is part of a wave of payments companies seeking to form banks. Others include pay later provider Affirm Holdings, which sought FDIC and Nevada bank charters this year, as well as mega-processor Fiserv and digital juggernaut Stripe, which have won special Georgia bank charters.

Miller doesn’t anticipate the company’s balance sheet approach changing if it does win the option to establish the bank.

“We continue to expect to be generally balance sheet light,” she said. “We're going to make choices around what the right return profile will be around when we keep it on balance sheet versus when we take it off.”

She didn’t provide any update on regulators’ response to the company’s application.

Block subsidiary Cash App has partnered with luxury apparel and footwear brand Nahmias to create a bandana that enables digital payments, the Oakland, California-based peer-to-peer payments provider said in a Monday press release.

The bandana has the payment company’s tap-to-pay tag, which lets customers pay without using their phones or wallets. The cotton and silk bandana features Cash App’s patch woven in a corner, indicating where users can tap to make contactless payments, the release said.

The two companies will begin selling the accessory exclusively through Cash App for $85 starting Nov. 17, per the release.

As Cash App expands its payment capabilities to uncommon objects, digital wallets are extending their offerings beyond cardless payments. And it’s not the only payments player to tap inanimate objects as payment tools: tech company Apple offers Apple Pay options for its proprietary watches.

Payment players like Google and Apple are allowing for personal documents to be tucked into digital wallets, letting users carry virtual driver’s licenses, passports, airline boarding passes and concert tickets. 

Along with integrating more personal documents into digital wallets, payment companies are increasingly relying on biometrics to execute transactions. Earlier this year, Clover, the Fiserv subsidiary, began providing its biometric verification services to Fiserv merchants, enabling consumers to pay with their face and palms.

We've intervened and Ethica Resolve Limited (Ethica), an FCA authorised firm that services and collects debt on behalf of creditors, has agreed to restrictions. These follow demands it made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes. 

  

            						

Ethica is acting on behalf of West 28th Street Limited (West 28), which bought disguised remuneration loans from a third party. West 28 is not authorised or regulated by the FCA.

Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries. HMRC has published guidance for those affected.

Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they're unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.

Under the requirements we’ve agreed, Ethica:

Will write to affected consumers, explaining that they do not have an enforceable obligation to make payment at this stage. (This means they do not need to pay now while regulatory and legal issues relating to the purported loans are resolved.)

Will not make further demands for payment from affected consumers in the current proposed court claim while regulatory and legal issues are resolved.

Additionally, Ethica and West 28 will not ask a court to make a judgment against someone who has not responded to a legal claim. This is known as a ‘default judgment’.  

However, consumers should not ignore any formal court documents they receive on this issue. They should consider seeking independent legal or debt advice before deciding what to do.

Additional protections for vulnerable consumers are being put in place and Ethica will identify affected consumers who may be vulnerable.

It has not yet been decided whether the debts can be enforced, which may be decided by a court.  

The requirements agreed protect consumers from avoidable harm while the relevant regulatory and legal issues are resolved.  

Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.

fullText:
The UK's most innovative businesses often start small.

Before they can develop new technologies, win contracts or expand into new markets, they need access to banking services to help them operate, invest and grow.

Access to financial services can be easy to take for granted. When those services work well they're almost invisible. However, when access becomes difficult or delayed, the effects can extend far beyond a single business.

Small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in or providing services to the defence sector play an important role in innovation and growth.

But these businesses do more than contribute to economic growth. Many are helping to develop the technologies, expertise and capabilities that support the UK's national resilience and security.

Banking services are part of that story. They help businesses secure contracts, invest in new opportunities and grow. They are one of the key links between innovation and capability, and between economic growth and national resilience.

That's why we wanted to understand whether defence SMEs were able to access banking services efficiently and consistently.

The challenge for defence SMEs is friction and delay, not exclusion

The current debate around defence and financial services has, at times, suggested that defence businesses are routinely excluded from accessing financial services. But for everyday banking services, such as opening a bank account, the picture is a lot more nuanced.

The firms we engaged with can and do serve defence SMEs. Many are taking steps to better understand and support the sector. In some cases, they're investing in specialist expertise, dedicated teams and governance processes.

But we also heard about long onboarding processes, repeated requests for information and delays in decision-making.

The theme that emerged was friction and delay rather than widespread exclusion.

That distinction matters because it points to a different challenge. The question is not whether firms are willing to serve the sector, but whether their processes are proportionate to the risks. And whether firms can reduce friction while managing risk effectively. SMEs can also help by being prepared to explain how they manage the risks associated with their business, and by providing clear and timely information to firms.

Defence is not one-size-fits-all

There is no regulatory barrier preventing firms from supporting lawful defence businesses. Financial services firms are entitled to make commercial decisions and determine their own risk appetite. But the approach they take should be proportionate to the specific risks.

One of the strongest messages from our work is that defence should not be viewed as a single category.

The sector is vast. It includes businesses that directly support the UK's defence capabilities, as well as those that are linked through the products, services or technologies they provide including software, logistics, maintenance, engineering, manufacturing and consulting. Their activities, business models and risk profiles can differ significantly.

Whatever the business model, robust due diligence to manage financial crime and other risks remains essential. But effective risk management is also about recognising differences.

A risk-based approach should focus on the specific customer, the activities they undertake and the risks they present.

Better information leads to better decisions

Another theme that stood out was the importance of data.

Many firms told us they do not always have a clear picture of their defence customers or the outcomes those customers experience throughout their journey with the firm.

Without good information, it becomes harder for firms to answer important questions including:

Are applications taking longer than expected?

Are decisions being applied consistently?

Do governance processes reflect actual risk?

Are customers receiving outcomes that align with the firm's stated approach?

Good management information helps firms answer those questions. It supports stronger oversight, better decision-making and ultimately better customer outcomes.

Getting the balance right

Our work does not introduce new rules or requirements. But it does reinforce an important principle: firms should take risk-based and proportionate decisions based on the circumstances of individual customers, including SMEs.

When firms get that balance right, they can manage risk effectively while helping viable businesses access the services they need to invest, innovate and grow.

Ultimately, we hope this work helps firms strike that balance and ensures that businesses contributing to the UK's national resilience can access the banking services they need to succeed.

Trade groups filed lawsuits against bank and credit union regulators over a preemption of a state law that bans swipe fees for taxes and tips.
